<meta>This page contains commentaries on Chapter 48 and the beginning of Chapter 49 of the Tao Te Ching. The commentators include Su Zhe (Su Zhu), Lü Huiqing (Lü Zhu), Huang Maocai, and Xizhai (Li Jia).</meta>

<margin>Su's Commentary <note>Su Zhe, 1039–1112 AD, a prominent Song dynasty official and scholar.</note></margin> Those who do not know the <term>Dao</term> <gloss>the Way</gloss> but devote themselves to learning will find that what they hear and see increases daily. Without a single principle to unify this knowledge, they cannot avoid it becoming a burden. Confucius said: "Hear much, select what is good and follow it; see much and remember it. This is the second level of knowledge." <note>A reference to the Analects 7:27.</note> If one day a person knows the <term>Dao</term>, they will look back at their previous false actions and realize that none were not delusions. Removing delusions to return to one's true nature is called "decreasing." Confucius asked Zigong: "Do you think I am one who learns much and remembers it all?" Zigong replied: "Yes, is it not so?" Confucius said: "No, I unify it all with a single thread." <note>Reference to Analects 15:3. The "single thread" implies a unifying spiritual principle rather than an accumulation of facts.</note> Forgetting the mind to return purely to one's nature is what is meant by "decreasing." If delusions still remain, one must continue until both the delusions and the act of forgetting are themselves forgotten. Once the mind returns purely to nature without any remainder, then one eliminates "doing" <note>purposive, ego-driven action</note> and does not fail to reach <term>wu wei</term> <gloss>non-action or effortless action</gloss>. All people have the desire to take hold of the world and finish its affairs; thus, they create business and seek after things. When their intentions are visible externally, things <note>others, or the world at large</note> will dislike them, making success difficult. The Sage practices non-action and therefore has no "business" in his heart. When his heart is visible externally, things are at peace with him. Although he does not try to take hold of the world's affairs, the world's affairs naturally follow and find peace through him.

<margin>Lü's Commentary <note>Lü Huiqing, 1032–1111 AD, a key figure in the New Policies of the Song dynasty.</note></margin> Practicing learning is for those who have not yet heard the <term>Dao</term>. Seeking it without having heard it requires breadth, hence it is said "one gains daily." Practicing the <term>Dao</term> is for those who have already heard the <term>Dao</term>. Having heard it and acting upon it requires nothing more than non-action, hence it is said "one decreases daily." To "decrease and further decrease" means one has not yet escaped the realm of "doing." Only by decreasing even the act of decreasing does one arrive at <term>wu wei</term> <gloss>non-action</gloss>. Non-action refers to being still and unmoving. "Nothing left undone" refers to being moved and subsequently penetrating the causes of all under heaven. Arriving at non-action through the process of non-action is what is called the Constant. Learning without worry is called divine; the direction of the divine is what is called the <term>Dao</term>. As for the ultimate divine, who can compare to this? From this perspective, taking the world is always done through non-action. As for using "doing" <note>purposive action</note>, it is clear that this is insufficient to take the world.

<column-break/>

<margin>Huang Maocai's Commentary <note>A Southern Song dynasty scholar known for his work on the Laozi.</note></margin> Only after there is nothing one does not know can one speak of learning; therefore, learning desires a daily increase. Only after there is nothing one does not do can one speak of the <term>Dao</term>; therefore, the <term>Dao</term> desires a daily decrease. However, increase can be sought through progress, while decrease is sometimes difficult to achieve through force. Only the most enlightened can suddenly drop everything and reach the realm of non-action. Thus they can leave nothing undone, and their practical application is inexhaustible, applied to the world with great ease.

<margin>Xizhai's Commentary <note>Li Jia, also known by his pseudonym Xizhai.</note></margin> Practicing learning is the means to seek knowledge, so it increases daily. Practicing the <term>Dao</term> is the means to remove delusion, so it decreases daily. If knowledge is not ultimate, then the decrease will not be complete. Thus, daily increase serves as the foundation for daily decrease. If one decreases and further decreases until delusion is gone and truth is whole, then one reaches non-action. When one reaches non-action, then every instance of "doing" is never anything other than "non-doing." This state cannot easily be discussed in terms of increase or decrease. When non-action reaches its ultimate point, even with the vastness of the world, one unifies it with a single thread. If one uses "busyness" <note>interfering action</note> to create more business, then even a single object beforehand will be sticky, entangled, and wrong, let alone the vastness of the world.

# Chapter 49

The Sage has no fixed heart <note>or mind</note>; he takes the heart of the people as his own. Those who are good, I treat as good. Those who are not good, I also treat as good; thus, virtue is goodness. Those who are faithful, I trust. Those who are not faithful, I also trust; thus, virtue is trust. The Sage lives in the world in a state of convergence, making his heart muddled for the sake of the world. The people all focus their ears and eyes on him; the Sage <note>The text cuts off here and continues on the next page.</note>

<summary>This page contains multiple commentaries on the Tao Te Ching's philosophy of "daily increase" in learning versus "daily decrease" in the Dao, leading to non-action. It also begins Chapter 49, describing the Sage's impartial treatment of all people regardless of their goodness or faithfulness.</summary>
